name: The Drafting Room
goal: Break a stated problem into functions before writing any of them.

description.what: How to turn a problem written in a paragraph of English into a short list of named functions, and how to write those names down before you write a single line that does any work.
description.why: Almost nobody is defeated by Python itself; they are defeated by staring at a problem too big to hold in their head all at once. Splitting it into named pieces makes each piece small enough to write, small enough to check on its own, and small enough to fix when it turns out to be wrong.
description.enables: Read a paragraph describing a task, list the separate jobs inside it, give each one a name and a signature, and then fill them in one at a time until the whole thing works.
description.assumes: You can write a function with parameters and a return value, call one function from inside another, use `if` and loops, and read a traceback when something fails.
description.assessed: You will be handed problems as paragraphs of prose with no structure suggested, and you will have to decide what the pieces are, name them, and make them work together.

sections.title: A paragraph hides several jobs
sections.body:
Here is a problem, written the way problems are actually given to you.

**A theatre sells tickets. A ticket costs 12 pounds, except for anyone under 16, who pays 7. An order of 5 tickets or more gets 10 per cent off the whole order. Report the amount owed, rounded to two decimal places.**

That one paragraph contains four separate decisions: what one ticket costs, how many tickets there are, whether a discount applies, and how the answer should be rounded. Each of those is a **job**. A job is a question the program has to answer that you could ask on its own and get a sensible reply to - "what does one ticket cost for a ten-year-old?" is a fair question by itself, while "what is the third line of the calculation?" is not.

The code below answers all four questions in one lump. It is correct, and it is still the wrong shape. If the discount rule changes you must read the whole function to find the two lines that care. If you want to check only the pricing rule, you cannot: there is nothing you can call that answers only that. Everything the function knows is trapped inside it.

Finding the jobs is a reading exercise, not a typing exercise, and it happens **before** any code exists. Read the paragraph and write the jobs down as short phrases, in whatever order they occur to you.

annotations.text: Job one, buried: deciding the price of a single ticket. There is no way to ask this question on its own - you can only ask it by pricing a whole order.
Job three, buried: the discount rule. `0.9` is the entire rule, and it is one keystroke away from being wrong with nothing to warn you.
Job four: rounding. Small, but a real decision - money arithmetic on a computer produces amounts such as 30.599999999999998, and rounding is what stops one of those reaching a customer.

checkpoint.prompt: The same theatre problem, with the first job pulled out into a function of its own. Fill in the two blanks so that `order_total(10, 3)` gives 21 and `order_total(40, 3)` gives 36.
checkpoint.explain: The tempting second blank is `age`, because `age` is the word you have just been thinking about. But `ticket_price(age)` has already finished with the age - it handed back a price, and a price is multiplied by a number of tickets. Once a job is behind a name you stop carrying its ingredients around with you, and that relief is most of what decomposition buys.

sections.title: A name is a promise
sections.body:
A function's name is the only part of it most readers will ever look at. If the name is honest they never need to open it; if the name lies, they will trust it and be wrong. Naming is not decoration, it is the surface everyone else touches.

Three habits cover nearly every case. A function that **works something out** takes a noun or noun phrase for the thing it hands back: `ticket_price`, `total_seconds`, `grade_for`. A function that **does something** takes a verb: `print_receipt`, `save_score`. A function that answers **yes or no** reads as a question, conventionally starting `is_` or `has_`, so that `if is_adult(age):` reads as English at the place it is used.

One test catches most bad names: if you cannot name the function without the word "and", it is two functions. `calculate_and_print_total` is a confession, not a name. Names like `data`, `do_it`, `helper`, `process` and `calc2` are the same confession said more quietly - they are what you write when you have not yet decided what the thing is.

Names are read far more often than they are typed, so spend the extra characters. `n` is fine for a counter inside three lines of loop; it is not fine for a function the rest of the program depends on.

annotations.text: A yes-or-no question named as a question. Its body is a single comparison, which looks far too small to deserve a function - until line 13.
Here is the payoff. `if is_discounted(2):` says what the rule means; `if 2 >= 5:` says only what it does. The name is where the meaning of that 5 now lives.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `is_adult(age)`, which hands back `True` when somebody is 18 or over and `False` otherwise.
checkpoint.hint: A comparison such as `age >= 18` is already `True` or `False`, so it can be handed straight back - no `if` is needed.
checkpoint.explain: Writing `if age >= 18: return True` followed by `else: return False` is not wrong, only noisy: the comparison is already the answer. The name matters more than the body here - because it is called `is_adult` rather than `check` or `age_test`, every line that calls it explains itself, and the number 18 is written down in exactly one place where it can be changed.

sections.title: One job, one reason to change
sections.body:
"One job" sounds vague until you turn it into a question with a real answer: **what would make me edit this function?** If there are two unrelated answers, there are two functions living in one.

The commonest example, and the one that costs beginners the most time, is a function that works something out and then prints it. That is two jobs - deciding, and announcing - so it has two reasons to change: the sum could change, or the wording could change. Worse, its answer is unusable. `print` puts characters on a screen and hands back nothing, so whoever called it receives `None` and cannot add to it, compare it, or check it. Every reuse you might want is blocked by that one line.

The repair is always the same shape: the function **returns** the value, and whoever called it decides what to do with it. One function can then serve a receipt, a running total and a check, without knowing that any of them exist.

The same split wears other disguises: a function that asks the user for input and then calculates, or one that calculates and then writes a file. Deciding is one job. Talking to the outside world is another. Keep them apart and the deciding half becomes something you can examine on its own.
sections.code:
def price_for_age(age):
    if age < 16:
        return 7
    return 12

# Two jobs in one: working the total out AND announcing it.
def show_total(age, count):
    total = price_for_age(age) * count
    print("Total: " + str(total))

# Split apart: this one only decides.
def total_for(age, count):
    return price_for_age(age) * count

show_total(30, 2)
print("Total: " + str(total_for(30, 2)))
print(total_for(30, 2) + total_for(10, 1))

annotations.text: `print` hands back nothing at all, so the call `show_total(30, 2)` is worth `None`. The number was computed and then thrown away.
`str(...)` turns a number into text so it can be joined onto a string with `+`. The wording now lives at the place the value is used, which is where wording belongs.
This line is impossible with `show_total`, and it is the whole argument for returning: values can be combined, printed characters cannot.

checkpoint.prompt:
Somebody wrote this and cannot work out why `total_with_tax(100, 0.2) + 5` fails.

`def total_with_tax(amount, rate):`
`    print(round(amount * (1 + rate), 2))`

Write `total_with_tax(amount, rate)` so that it hands back the amount plus that rate of tax, rounded to two decimal places, instead.
checkpoint.solution:
def total_with_tax(amount, rate):
    return round(amount * (1 + rate), 2)
checkpoint.hint: The arithmetic is already right. Change only what happens to the result: hand it back rather than putting it on the screen.
checkpoint.explain: The original looks like it works, because the right number does appear on the screen - which is exactly why this trap catches people. Nothing is wrong with the calculation; the fault is that the value was spent on a display and never given to the caller, so what actually runs is `None + 5`. A function that returns can always be printed by its caller, whereas a function that prints can never be un-printed.

sections.title: Write the empty shapes first
sections.body:
Here is the working order that makes all of this practical, and it is deliberately backwards from how it feels.

First, list the jobs. Second, write a `def` line for each with the parameters you think it needs and a **docstring** - a plain sentence in triple quotes as the first line of the body - saying what it hands back. Give it a body of `pass`, which is Python's way of saying "nothing here yet" so that the file still runs. That empty shell is called a **stub**. Third, write the top-level function as nothing but calls to those names, and read it aloud: if the sentence it makes is true, your decomposition is right. Only then, fourth, fill in one stub at a time, checking each before starting the next.

What this buys is that you meet your mistakes early and one at a time. Discovering at the stub stage that `discount_factor` also needs the price costs you ten seconds; discovering it after eighty lines costs an afternoon. And when a filled-in function misbehaves you know which one, because the others were working before you touched it.

The last step, calling small functions from a larger one to build the answer, is called **composing** them. Notice below that `order_total` contains no pricing rule at all - it says only how the pieces fit together. A function whose job is to combine other functions is doing one job too.

annotations.text: The docstring is written before the body exists. If you cannot write this sentence, you do not yet know what the function is - a far cheaper thing to discover now than later.
This began life as a `def` line followed by `pass`. Handing back a multiplier rather than an already-discounted price keeps the rule separate from the sum it is applied to.
The composing line. Every rule from the paragraph lives in exactly one function, so the theatre changing its discount touches one line in one place.

checkpoint.prompt: Put the four steps of the stubs-first working order into the order you would actually carry them out.
fragments: Write a def line and a docstring for each job, with `pass` as the body
Fill in one function at a time, checking each before starting the next
Read the problem and write down each separate job it contains
Write the top-level function as calls to those names, and read it aloud
checkpoint.explain: The tempting order fills the small functions in before the top-level one is written, because that feels like doing the real work first. It is the expensive order: until the top-level function exists you do not know what the small ones must hand back, so you write several of them twice. Settling the shape while it is still free is the entire point of stubs.

guided-practice.prompt:
A number of seconds should be reported as text: 3661 becomes `1h 1m 1s`, and 59 becomes `0h 0m 59s`.

Three stubs are waiting for you, one per job. Fill them in and let `duration_text` compose them. Recall that `//` is whole-number division and `%` is the remainder, so `130 // 60` is 2 and `130 % 60` is 10.
guided-practice.hint: Hours are `total // 3600`. For the minutes, first throw the whole hours away with `total % 3600`, then divide what is left by 60.
guided-practice.explain: The minutes stub is where this is won or lost: `total // 60` counts every minute in the whole duration, including the ones already reported as hours, so 3661 would come out as `1h 61m 1s`. Taking the remainder first is what makes the three answers add back up to the original rather than overlapping. The docstrings were written before the bodies precisely so this distinction - complete minutes against leftover minutes - was settled in English before it had to be settled in arithmetic.

guided-practice.prompt:
**A cinema charges 9 pounds a ticket, or 5 for anyone under 14. An order of 4 tickets or more takes 15 per cent off the whole order. Report the amount owed, rounded to two decimal places.**

The jobs are the price of one ticket, the discount an order size earns, and the total that combines them. Fill in a function for each and let `order_total(age, count)` compose them.
guided-practice.hint: 15 per cent off means you keep 85 per cent, so the multiplier is `0.85`. `order_total` should contain no prices and no percentages of its own - only calls and a `round`.
guided-practice.explain: The boundaries are where the paragraph must be read exactly: 13 is under 14 so it pays 5, and 4 tickets counts as "4 or more" so it does earn the discount. Both are the kind of off-by-one a single lump of code hides and separate functions expose, because `discount_factor(4)` can be asked on its own. Notice too that `round` appears once, in the composing function - rounding each piece separately would give a different and wronger answer.

guided-practice.prompt: `average_of` is doing two jobs and the second has eaten the first: `average_of(3, 4, 5) + 1` fails with `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'`. Repair it so it hands back the mean of the three numbers.
guided-practice.hint: One word changes. Ask what the function should hand to whoever called it, and let them decide whether it goes on the screen.
guided-practice.explain: The traceback says `NoneType` because a function with no `return` hands back `None`: the mean was worked out, written to the screen, and discarded. The temptation is to add a `return` while keeping the `print`, which passes these tests and leaves the function still doing two jobs - it would then chatter into the output of every program that ever calls it. Deciding and announcing stay apart.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete this stub. The docstring is already written, so the name and the placeholder body are all that is missing: the name should say what the docstring promises, and the body should be the keyword meaning "nothing here yet".
guided-practice.explain: `leap_year` or `check_year` would run perfectly well, but a function handing back True or False reads best as a question, so that `if is_leap(year):` is a sentence at the place it is used. The body has to be `pass` rather than empty: Python refuses a `def` with no body at all, and `pass` is what lets an unfinished file still run so you can check the shape before writing any rules.

guided-practice.prompt:
Here is a function somebody wrote for a shop.

`def checkout(price, quantity):`
`    total = price * quantity`
`    if quantity >= 10:`
`        total = total * 0.9`
`    print("You owe " + str(round(total, 2)))`

Name the separate jobs hiding in it, and say what goes wrong when the shop later wants the same total shown somewhere else with different wording.
guided-practice.hint: Ask what would make you edit this function. A change to the discount would; a change to the sentence on the receipt would as well. That is two reasons.
guided-practice.explain: It has at least two reasons to change - the pricing rule and the wording - and because the result is printed rather than returned, the second display cannot reuse the first calculation at all. It would have to copy the arithmetic, and copied arithmetic is how a shop ends up running two different discount rules by accident. The repair is one function that returns the total and another that turns a total into a sentence.

independent-practice.prompt:
**A car park charges nothing for the first 30 minutes. After that it charges 2.50 for every hour that has been started, so 31 minutes costs 2.50 and 61 minutes costs 5.00. No stay ever costs more than 15.00.**

Write the plan you would work from, before any code exists. For each piece of work, give the name you would give it, what it is handed, what it hands back, and the single job it does in one sentence. Then say which sentence of the paragraph ended up in which piece.
independent-practice.explain: The three rules in that paragraph are independent of one another - the free period, the started-hour charge, and the ceiling - and that independence is the signal that each deserves its own name. A plan with one piece per rule can be checked rule by rule against the prose, and any sentence of prose you cannot point at in your plan is a rule you have not implemented. Plans that describe steps of a calculation instead, such as "work out the minutes, then multiply", tend to collapse back into one lump, because a step of arithmetic cannot be asked as a question on its own.

independent-practice.prompt: Make that car park work. `parking_charge(minutes)` hands back what a stay of this many minutes costs: nothing at all for 30 minutes or less, otherwise 2.50 for every hour that has been started, and never more than 15.00.
independent-practice.explain: Exactly 60 minutes has started one hour and exactly 61 has started two, which is the boundary that plain division gets wrong in one direction or the other. The ceiling has to be applied after the multiplication rather than to the hours, because it is stated in pounds and not in hours: capping the hours at six agrees with these tests today and disagrees the day the rate changes. Rules written as separate functions can each be read back against the sentence of prose that produced them, which is how you notice that.

independent-practice.prompt:
**A mark out of 100 earns a grade: A from 70, B from 60, C from 50, and F below that. A mark of 50 or more is a pass.** `grade_report(mark)` hands back one line of text in exactly this form.

`Mark 72: grade A, pass`
`Mark 41: grade F, fail`
independent-practice.explain: Three jobs live in that paragraph and only one of them is obvious: the grade letter, the pass decision, and the sentence presenting both. Working the pass out from the letter - treating F as the only failure - happens to agree with today's thresholds and quietly breaks the moment the pass mark and the C boundary stop coinciding, which is the difference between a rule you read and a rule you inferred. Building the sentence in its own place also means the wording can change without anyone going near the thresholds.

independent-practice.prompt: `basket_total(2, 3, 4, 5)` should give 26, and instead fails with `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'NoneType'`. Repair the program so the total comes back to whoever asked for it.
independent-practice.explain: Both sides of the `+` are `None` because both calls printed and handed nothing back, and the message names both operands, which tells you the fault is in the function they share. The tempting repair is to abandon `line_total` and do the multiplication twice inside `basket_total`; that passes, and it throws away the one function worth keeping, so the next basket with three lines starts from nothing. A small function that returns can be reused; the same one printing is a dead end.

exam.prompt: A function has one job when there is only one reason you would ever edit it. Which of these has more than one?
choices: `postage_for(grams)`, which returns the postage due on a parcel of that weight
`save_and_report(score)`, which writes the score to a file and prints a confirmation
`is_weekend(day)`, which returns True for Saturday and Sunday
`seconds_between(start, end)`, which returns how many seconds separate two times
exam.explain: The "and" in its name is the confession: the file format could change, or the confirmation wording could change, and either sends you into the same function. The other three each answer a single question and hand back a single value, however much arithmetic that takes inside - length of body is not what one job means.

choices: A function that has been written and checked but is not called anywhere yet
A short function of one or two lines that a longer function calls
A function's `def` line and docstring with `pass` as its body, written before the real body exists
A comment describing code you intend to write later
exam.explain: The second option tempts because small functions and stubs often look alike, but a stub is defined by being unfinished, not by being small - it exists so the shape of a program can be run and read before any of the work is done. A comment cannot do that job, because a comment cannot be called and so can never prove the pieces fit together.

exam.prompt:
What does this program print?

`def double(n):`
`    return n * 2`

`def add_ten(n):`
`    return n + 10`

`def transform(n):`
`    return add_ten(double(n))`

`print(transform(5))`
`print(double(add_ten(5)))`
exam.explain: The inner call runs first and its result becomes the outer call's argument, so the first line doubles and then adds, while the second adds and then doubles. Both lines use the same two functions and give different answers, which is why the order of composition is a decision in its own right rather than a detail of layout.

exam.prompt:
What does this program print?

`def add(a, b):`
`    return a + b`

`def show(a, b):`
`    print(a + b)`

`x = add(2, 3)`
`y = show(4, 5)`
`print(x)`
`print(y)`
exam.explain: The 9 appears first, before either `print` at the bottom, because `show` prints while it is running instead of handing anything back. `y` is therefore `None`, the value of a function that returns nothing, and that `None` is the whole reason a printing function cannot be built on. Assuming the 9 came from `print(y)` is the trap.

exam.prompt: The docstring is already written. Fill in the name it promises and the number that makes the body honest.
exam.explain: The docstring is the specification, so the name is read off it rather than invented: it hands back a number of seconds, so it is named for that. 60 is the tempting second blank because 60 is the number already on the line, but hours reach seconds through two conversions rather than one.

exam.prompt: You have been handed a problem in a paragraph. Put these four actions into the order that costs you the least work.
fragments: Write the top-level function as calls to names that do not exist yet, and check it reads correctly
Fill in one function at a time, checking each before starting the next
Read the paragraph and write down each separate job it contains
Write a def line, a docstring and a `pass` body for each job
exam.explain: Every step before the last is reversible in seconds, which is exactly why they come first: a wrong parameter list costs nothing to change while the body is still `pass`. Filling functions in before the top-level one exists is the natural instinct and the expensive order, because you are then guessing what each must hand back instead of reading it off the place it is used.

exam.prompt:
`abs(n)` gives the size of a number with any minus sign removed. Work through the calls this program makes.

`def clean(n):`
`    return abs(n)`

`def scale(n):`
`    return n * 3`

`def prepare(n):`
`    return scale(clean(n))`

`print(prepare(-4))`
exam.explain: `prepare` contains no arithmetic of its own; every value in this trace was produced by one of the two small functions, and `prepare` decides only the order they run in. That is what makes composed code easy to follow - each step of the trace has exactly one function to blame if it is wrong. Answering -12 anywhere means the sign was carried past `clean`, which is the one job `clean` exists to do.

exam.prompt: Why is a function that prints its result harder to build on than one that returns it? Answer in two or three sentences.
exam.explain: Printing sends characters to the screen and hands back `None`, so the value itself is gone: the caller cannot add it to anything, compare it, or check it. Returning leaves the decision about display to whoever called, which is why one returning function can serve a screen, a file and a check at once, while a printing one serves only the screen.

exam.prompt: **A parcel costs 3.00 to send if it weighs 1000 grams or less. Every additional started kilogram adds 2.00, so 1001 grams costs 5.00 and 3000 grams costs 7.00. Express delivery doubles whatever the parcel would otherwise cost.** Write `shipping_total(grams, express)`, where `express` is True or False.
exam.hint: Two questions live in here: what the parcel costs by weight, and what express does to a cost. Answer them in separate functions and the doubling never has to know about kilograms.
exam.explain: 2500 grams is 1500 grams over the first kilogram, which is two started kilograms rather than one and a half - rounding down there gives 12.00 and looks entirely plausible. Keeping the express rule out of the weight calculation is what makes such a slip cheap to fix: express doubles a cost, whatever that cost happens to be, so it never needs to see a weight at all.

exam.prompt: `plot_summary(2, 3)` should give 16 - an area of 6 plus a fence of 10 - and instead fails with `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'`. Repair it.
exam.hint: Only one of the two small functions is lying about its result. The message says which side of the `+` is empty.
exam.explain: `width * height` is worked out and then dropped on the floor, because a line that is only an expression changes nothing - the missing word is `return`, not a missing calculation. The traceback names `plot_summary`, which is where the failure surfaced, while the fault is in `area`: `NoneType` on the left of the `+` and `int` on the right says which of the two calls handed back nothing, and reading that is faster than reading either function.
